$$
56,\ 71,\ 120,\ 135,\ 184,\ 199,\ 248,\ 263,\ 312,\ 327,\ 376,\ 391,\ 440,\ 449,\ 450,\ 451,\ 452,\ 453,\ 454,\ 456,\ 464,\ 472,\ 480,\ 488,\ 496
$$

we first analyze the **differences between consecutive terms**:

$$
\begin{align*}
71 - 56 &= 15 \\
120 - 71 &= 49 \\
135 - 120 &= 15 \\
184 - 135 &= 49 \\
199 - 184 &= 15 \\
248 - 199 &= 49 \\
263 - 248 &= 15 \\
312 - 263 &= 49 \\

$$

We observe that the **differences alternate between 15 and 49**, starting with 15. This suggests a **periodic pattern** in the sequence.

---

### Step 1: Identify the Pattern

Let’s denote the sequence as $ a(n) $, where $ n \geq 0 $. The first few terms are:

$$
\begin{align*}
a(0) &= 56 \\
a(1) &= 71 \\
a(2) &= 120 \\
a(3) &= 135 \\
a(4) &= 184 \\
a(5) &= 199 \\

a(9) &= 327 \\

a(11) &= 391 \\
a(12) &= 440 \\
\end{align*}
$$

We can see that every **two steps**, the sequence increases by $ 15 + 49 = 64 $. That is:

$$
a(n) = a(n-2) + 64 \quad \text{for } n \geq 2
$$

This recurrence relation is valid for the first 13 terms (up to $ a(12) = 440 $).

---

### Step 2: Define the Recursive Formula

Given the observed pattern, we define the recursive formula as:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
a(0) &= 56 \\
a(1) &= 71 \\
a(n) &= a(n-2) + 64 \quad \text{for } n \geq 2
\end{aligned}
}
$$

This formula generates the sequence correctly up to $ a(12) = 440 $, and it is consistent with the alternating pattern of differences.

---

### Step 3: Optional Generalization

If we want to express the recurrence in terms of the previous term (not just two steps back), we can write:

$$
a(n) = a(n-1) + 
\begin{cases}
15 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \\
49 & \text{if } n \text{ is even}
\end{cases}
$$

This is also valid for $ n \geq 1 $, with $ a(0) = 56 $.

\begin{aligned}
a(0) &= 56 \\

a(n) &= a(n-2) + 64 \quad \text{for } n \geq 2
